National Register of Historic Places listings in Duval County, Florida

stops.name: Florida Theatre
stops.description: Elvis Presley played two nights here in August 1956 while a local judge sat in the audience with arrest warrants ready over his hips.

stops.name: Laura Street Trio
stops.description: Three empty landmarks on one corner, two of them Prairie School towers by Henry Klutho, waiting out a restoration that has been promised since 2010.

stops.name: St. James Building
stops.description: Built in 1912 as the Cohen Brothers department store and now Jacksonville City Hall, its glass dome is the biggest room Henry Klutho ever put under one roof.

stops.name: Barnett National Bank Building
stops.description: This 18 story bank tower of 1926 was the tallest thing in Florida for a decade and sat dark for twenty years before reopening as apartments and offices.

stops.name: Dyal-Upchurch Building
stops.description: The first multi-story building to rise from the ashes of the Great Fire of 1901, and the first thing Henry Klutho ever designed in this city.

stops.name: Basilica of the Immaculate Conception
stops.description: A Gothic Revival parish rebuilt after the 1901 fire and raised to minor basilica in 2013, one of only a handful in Florida.

stops.name: Morocco Temple
stops.description: Klutho built this Shriners hall in 1911 with Prairie School lines borrowed straight from Frank Lloyd Wright, and lawyers rent the upper floors today.

stops.name: James Weldon Johnson Park
stops.description: Jacksonville's oldest park, laid out in 1857 and renamed in 2020 for the hometown writer of "Lift Every Voice and Sing".

stops.name: Elks Club Building
stops.description: A lodge hall on the Laura Street spine, listed on the National Register as part of the downtown rebuild that followed the 1901 fire.

stops.name: Old St. Andrew's Episcopal Church
stops.description: An 1887 Gothic Revival church that outlived its congregation and now houses the Jacksonville Historical Society, across the street from the arena.

stops.name: Prime F. Osborn III Convention Center
stops.description: The Beaux-Arts hall behind those columns was Jacksonville Terminal, the largest railroad station in the South when it opened in 1919.

stops.name: Ritz Theatre and LaVilla Museum
stops.description: The heart of LaVilla, a Black neighborhood once billed as the Harlem of the South, rebuilt in Art Deco on the site of the 1929 Ritz.

stops.name: Friendship Fountain
stops.description: The world's largest fountain when it opened in 1965, throwing water 120 feet over the Southbank Riverwalk, and running again since a 2024 rebuild.

stops.name: Treaty Oak
stops.description: A live oak of roughly 250 years, saved from developers in the 1930s by a reporter who invented a story about peace treaties signed under it.

note: Jacksonville, FL had never been scouted; every other city in this file's history has had at least one run. 14 stops verified. The core twelve sit inside a half mile of Laura and Forsyth, with Friendship Fountain and the Treaty Oak reached over the Main Street Bridge on the Southbank, about eight minutes on foot from the north bank. The Laura Street Trio is the one stop with no street number: Wikipedia, the city's Downtown Investment Authority and every listing give it as the intersection of N Laura and W Forsyth rather than an address, so address and zip are left null instead of guessed, and its coordinates are supplied. It is also vacant and was sold to a new developer in August 2026, so it is a stop you look at rather than enter. Dropped: EverBank Stadium and the arena, which are venues rather than standable landmarks and sit off the walkable core; Gator Bowl Stadium, Jacksonville Landing, Wolfson Park and the Hotel George Washington, all demolished; the Skyway stations, the bridges and the office towers, which have articles but are not stops; Old City Cemetery and Bethel Baptist, which are real and listed but pull the loop too far north to keep the cluster tight.
